facts.text: On July 24, 2020, at 2:19 p.m., the Taipei weather station recorded 39.7°C.
The 39.7°C reading was the highest at the Taipei weather station since the station was set up in 1896.
In July 2020 Taipei had 17 days in a row with highs above 36°C, which was also a record.
Before 2020, Taipei's longest run of days above 36°C was 16 days, from August 5 to 20, 2017.
The weather agency said the July 2020 heat came from sinking air under a strong Pacific high, warm air from southern China, and the heat island effect in the Taipei Basin.
In July 2020, Taiwan's health ministry counted about 30% more heat injuries than a year earlier.
From 1910 to 2020, the number of very hot days rose at all six of Taiwan's century-old weather stations, and it rose the most at the Taipei station.
The six century-old weather stations are Taipei, Taichung, Tainan, Hengchun, Hualien and Taitung.
At the Taipei station, very hot days rose sharply after 1990 and set new records again and again after 2000.
In 2003, in 2016, 2017 and 2018, and in 2020, Taipei had more than 30 days at or above 36°C.
Taipei's daily highs are often the highest of the six stations, probably because the station sits in the middle of a basin that traps heat and in a crowded city with a heat island effect.
Taiwan's weather agency defined a high temperature as 35°C before 2018 and changed it to 36°C in 2018.
Taiwan's yearly average temperature rose by about 1.5°C from 1900 to 2022.
The summer of 2020 was the hottest season in the records of Taiwan's weather agency.
Taipei's yearly average temperature was 22.1°C in 1970 and 24.2°C in 2020.
Taipei's yearly average temperature was 2.1°C higher in 2020 than in 1970.
Every yearly average in Taipei from 2016 to 2025 was at least 23.5°C, while 1995 averaged 22.3°C.
